Name: Konark Sun Temple
Description / Significance: A 13th-century temple built in the form of a colossal stone chariot for the sun god Surya, with 24 carved wheels and a team of seven horses. It's Odisha's only UNESCO World Heritage Site, inscribed in 1984, and remains one of the most studied examples of Kalinga architecture anywhere.

Name: Jagannath Temple
Description / Significance: Built in 1161 CE, this is the spiritual center of Odisha and one of India's Char Dham pilgrimage sites. It's the starting point of the annual Rath Yatra and follows Kalinga temple architecture, with its 65-metre spire visible for miles.

Name: Lingaraj Temple
Description / Significance: One of the oldest and largest temples in the city, dedicated to Harihara (a combined form of Shiva and Vishnu). Its ASI protection covers nine minor shrines within the compound, making it a complex rather than a single structure.

Name: Mukteswar Temple
Description / Significance: Known as the "gem of Odishan architecture," this small 10th-century temple is famous for its ornately carved torana (arched gateway), considered one of the finest examples of stone carving in the region.

Name: Parsurameswar Temple
Description / Significance: Among the oldest surviving temples in the Old Town area, dating to roughly the 7th century, and one of the earliest examples of the classic Kalinga temple style still standing.

Name: Rajarani Temple
Description / Significance: Unusual among Odisha temples because it has no presiding deity inside — its significance lies entirely in its sculpture, especially graceful female figures carved along the tower.

Name: Brahmeswara Temple
Description / Significance: An 11th-century temple built by Kolavati Devi, mother of a Somavanshi king, notable for its cluster of minor shrines protected as one compound.

Name: Ananta Vasudeva Temple
Description / Significance: The only major Vaishnavite temple among Bhubaneswar's largely Shaivite temple cluster, indicating the coexistence of different devotional traditions in the same sacred landscape.

Name: Udayagiri and Khandagiri Caves
Description / Significance: Twin hills containing rock-cut monastic cells carved for Jain ascetics roughly 2,000 years ago, under the patronage of King Kharavela. They contain some of the earliest known Jain inscriptions in India.

Name: Dhauli Rock Edicts
Description / Significance: The site believed to mark where Emperor Ashoka's Kalinga War took place, after which he renounced violence and adopted Buddhism. The inscriptions here are unique for softening the harsher tone found in Ashoka's edicts elsewhere.

Name: Barabati Fort
Description / Significance: A largely ruined fortress that once served as the capital seat of the Gajapati kings, now surviving mainly as gateways and earthworks amid the modern city.

Name: Sisupalgarh
Description / Significance: One of the earliest and most extensively planned ancient cities in India, dating back over 2,500 years, with a grid layout and massive ramparts — historically significant far beyond its current physical condition.

Name: Chausath Yogini Temple
Description / Significance: A rare circular, roofless (hypaethral) temple dedicated to 64 yoginis, an unusual and much smaller counterpart to the larger Chausath Yogini temples found elsewhere in India.

Name: Chausath Jogini Temple
Description / Significance: Another of India's few surviving 64-yogini temples, with three additional minor shrines, reflecting a tantric worship tradition that has largely disappeared elsewhere.

Name: Ratnagiri Buddhist Site
Description / Significance: One of the largest Buddhist monastic complexes in eastern India, with three monasteries and hundreds of stupas, indicating this region was a major center of Buddhist learning centuries before Odisha became predominantly Vaishnavite.

Name: Lalitagiri (Naltigiri) Buddhist Ruins
Description / Significance: Considered among the oldest Buddhist establishments in Odisha, with ruins and relic caskets suggesting activity dating back to the Mauryan period.

Name: Udayagiri Buddhist Site
Description / Significance: Distinct from the Jain caves of the same name near Bhubaneswar, this is part of Odisha's "Diamond Triangle" of Buddhist sites alongside Ratnagiri and Lalitagiri.

Name: Pushpagiri Vihara
Description / Significance: A Buddhist monastic complex identified by some scholars as the historical Pushpagiri mentioned in ancient Chinese travelers' accounts, making it a site of ongoing archaeological interest.

Name: Athara Nala Bridge
Description / Significance: An 18-arch bridge over the Madhupur stream, historically significant as part of the old pilgrim route into Puri.

Name: Varahi Temple
Description / Significance: A temple dedicated to the goddess Varahi (a boar-headed form of Shakti), notable for being one of the few temples in the region dedicated specifically to this fierce tantric goddess.

Name: Asoka Rock Inscriptions
Description / Significance: A second major set of Ashokan edicts in Odisha (alongside Dhauli), confirming the extent of Mauryan administrative reach into ancient Kalinga.

Name: Mahendragiri Temple Group
Description / Significance: A hilltop cluster of temples (Bhima, Kunti, and Yudhistra) named after the Pandava brothers of the Mahabharata, linking local geography to epic tradition.

Name: Gandharadi Temples
Description / Significance: Home to the Nilamadhava and Sidheswara shrines, historically significant as Boudh district's major temple complex outside the main coastal temple circuit.

Name: Paschima Somnatha Group
Description / Significance: A cluster of temples including Bhubanesvara and Kapilesvara, representing the temple-building tradition of the inland Boudh kingdom, distinct from coastal Kalinga styles.

Name: Vikramkhol Rock Inscriptions
Description / Significance: Contains some of the earliest examples of proto-writing in the region, of ongoing interest to epigraphists studying the development of scripts in eastern India.

Name: Chandrasekhar Temple Group
Description / Significance: A hilltop temple complex reached by a long flight of ancient stone steps, historically an important pilgrimage site for Dhenkanal's local kingdom.

Name: Simhanatha Mahadeva Temple
Description / Significance: Located on a river island formed by the confluence of the Mahanadi and Birupa rivers, giving it a distinctive geographic setting unlike most Odisha temples.

Name: Ravana Chhaya Rock Paintings
Description / Significance: Contains rare rock paintings from the early historic period, among the very few surviving examples of ancient painting (rather than carving) in Odisha.

Name: Asurgarh Fort
Description / Significance: An ancient fort site associated with early regional kingdoms, providing archaeological evidence of settled political power in the Kalahandi region well before medieval records begin.

Name: Bhaskareswar Temple
Description / Significance:
A smaller Shiva temple in the Old Town cluster, notable for housing an unusually large monolithic lingam.
